new_statements.translation: [p.94] 1.4 Tones. Bidiya is a tone language. Three level-tone heights are distinguished, marked respectively high (v́), mid (v), low (v̀). Tones are written over the vowels. [pp.24-25] Bidiya uses pitch, which it organises into three distinct registers. There are thus three level tones (high, low and mid) with a distinctive function both on the [lexical and grammatical] plane ... [p.95] ... [loanwords of] Arabic or French origin whose stressed syllable is rendered by a falling tone: birmiil 'barrel', hijaaz 'pilgrimage', hijaab 'protection, amulet', 'ibiriik 'jug', làwwaày 'beam', ... 'bridge'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bidiya is analysed as a three-level tone language (H, M, L, plus M-L contour on certain CVV/CVC/CVVC shapes); tone is lexically and grammatically distinctive (verb classes, plural formation, readers nouns). The grammar has no section on word stress/accent and never posits one; the only reference to stress is that the stressed syllable of Arabic/French loanwords is nativised as a falling tone. 'Accent' appears in the book only as the name of the tone diacritics (p.25).
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal, not accentual: high tone is very rare (p.94, p.98: only 5 all-H isotone words in a 2909-item corpus; H practically absent from CVVC verbals and rare in absolute-final syllables of CVCV shapes); automatic M>ML 'modulation' on CVV/CVC/CVVC mid-tone words (p.96); final M realised on the high register before certain suffixed subject/possessive pronouns (p.98, 1.4.3.1); dialect bìgàwgùno differs tonally from the other four dialects (p.20).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical citation forms (1.4.1-1.4.2) and tones in the utterance (1.4.3 'Les tons dans l'énoncé', pp.98-105, tone sandhi rules 1.4.3.1-1.4.3.9). Access caveat: read through Google Books search-within-volume snippets (verbatim, page-numbered) rather than a full copy; the absence of any stress section is inferred from zero full-text hits for accentuation/accentué/intensité/proéminence/intonation and the single diacritic-only hit for 'accent'.
new_statements.identity_note: Alio 1986 describes Bidiya (bidi1241) as a whole, based mainly on the author's own dialect; he notes five mutually intelligible dialects and a tonal split between four of them and the 'bìgàwgùno' dialect (p.20). Fedry 1977 describes the Zerli parler of Bidiyo (p.89). No sub-glottocodes exist for these dialects.

sources.note: Sec. 1.4 'Les tons' (p.94): Bidiya is a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L), lexically and grammatically distinctive; p.24-25 same in the introduction; p.95: in Arabic/French loans the source-language stressed syllable is rendered by a falling tone. No word-stress/accent section: full-text probes for 'accentuation', 'accentué', 'intensité', 'proéminence', 'intonation' return 0 hits; 'accent' occurs once (p.25) only as the name of the acute/grave diacritics marking H and L tone.
